title: NIFTEM-K Hosts India–Canada Roundtable on Pulse Protein Innovation, Value Addition and Strategic Partnerships
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                13 OCT 2026 7:25PM by PIB Delhi
content:
National Institute of Food Technology Entrepreneurship and Management, Kundli (NIFTEM-K), an Institute of National Importance, under the Ministry of Food Processing Industries, Government of India, organised a Roundtable Conference on “Pulse Protein Innovation, Value Addition and Strategic Partnerships” on 13 October 2026. The conference brought together senior government representatives, academic leaders, industry associations and research organisations from India and Canada to strengthen bilateral cooperation in pulse protein innovation, food processing, research and sustainable nutrition.
The conference was attended by Mr. Ken Cheveldayoff, Hon’ble Minister of Advanced Education, Government of Saskatchewan, Canada, along with David Anderson, Managing Director, Government of Saskatchewan, and Harish Vaidyanathan, Senior Trade Officer, Saskatchewan India Office. The University of Saskatchewan (USask) delegation included Dr. Baljit Singh, Vice-President (Research); Dr. Trever Crowe, Associate Dean (Research and Graduate Studies); Dr. Ajay Dalai, Professor; and Dr. Supratim Ghosh, Professor.
Industry and research organisations were represented by Greg Cherewyk, President, Pulse Canada; Julianne Curran, Vice-President (Market Innovation), Pulse Canada; Carl Potts, Executive Director, Saskatchewan Pulse Growers; Leanne Fischbuch, Executive Director, Alberta Pulse Growers; Bob Behari, CEO, Enviroway; and Prachi Kaul, Director, Shastri Indo-Canadian Institute. Representatives of Indian organisations and industry, including Nutrition International, Nutricircle, India Pulses and Grains Association, ICAR–Indian Institute of Pulses Research, Kanpur, the International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT), Diet Foods, Good Food Institute India and IIT Delhi, also participated in the discussions.
In his address, Hon. Ken Cheveldayoff highlighted the importance of India–Saskatchewan relations and the value of personal connections in strengthening ties between India and Canada. He underlined the opportunities for closer cooperation in higher education, research, innovation and academic exchange, noting the potential for institutions and industry to work together on shared priorities.
Dr. Harinder Singh Oberoi, Director, NIFTEM-K, emphasised the importance of translating the points mentioned in the Memorandum of Understanding between NIFTEM-K and the University of Saskatchewan into tangible outcomes. He stated that the partnership should move beyond the agreement to a clear, time-bound programme of action that delivers meaningful benefits for both countries. He expressed his gratitude to all the stakeholders and expressed satisfaction about the significant progress made during the short period of about seven months after the MoU was signed. He highlighted the goal of working towards establishing the joint Centre of Excellence at NIFTEM-K within the next year, supported by a practical roadmap, defined milestones and institutional coordination.
The discussions also recognised key challenges in pulse processing and protein ingredient development. These include ensuring consistency in raw materials and ingredients, managing process energy requirements and energy use, optimising processing conditions, and preserving or improving the functional properties of pulse proteins. Participants also highlighted the importance of addressing texture-related challenges and developing fit-for-purpose pulse-based ingredients that can support value addition and the development of innovative food products.
Dr. Oberoi further stressed that the partners should identify priority research areas and agree on an actionable plan for the first two years. Potential areas of collaboration include pulse protein extraction and processing, value addition, development of innovative and nutritious food products, joint research projects and publications, joint PhD degree programme, student and faculty exchanges, training programmes, and collaborative research funding. He also highlighted the importance of industry participation to help translate research into scalable technologies, commercial products and wider market opportunities.
Dr. Baljit Singh while expressing satisfaction over the progress made by both the University of Saskatchewan (USask) and NIFTEM-K mentioned that USask has identified PhD students who will do part of their research work at NIFTEM-K. He also stated that a collaborative project entitled “ Sustainable health innovation in fortification (lentils) for SDG 2.2 (end all forms of malnutrition), has been submitted by USask in collaboration with NIFTEM-K and other international partners for funding by Government of Canada. The roundtable coordinated by Dr. Baljit Singh provided a platform for academic and industry stakeholders to discuss research collaboration, capacity building, technology development and commercialisation. Participants explored opportunities to develop value-added pulse-based foods, strengthen links between researchers and businesses, and address emerging needs in sustainable and plant-based nutrition. The discussions also focused on creating a coordinated framework through which research priorities, expertise and facilities in India and Canada can complement each other.
The conference forms part of the broader effort to advance the joint Centre of Excellence, with NIFTEM-K and the University of Saskatchewan serving as co-chairs of the initiative, as stated in the conference background. The proposed collaboration is intended to bring together academic expertise, government support and industry engagement to advance pulse protein innovation and strengthen research and educational links between the two countries.
The roundtable concluded with an emphasis on converting the discussions into defined priorities, responsibilities and timelines. The proposed roadmap and two-year research priorities are expected to provide a foundation for sustained institutional cooperation and measurable progress in pulse protein research, value addition and innovation, further strengthening India–Canada academic, scientific and industry partnerships.

Under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, India is moving forward with the spirit of ‘Vishwamitra’  and has always remained committed to peace, coexistence, and human welfare

In line with vision of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, it is our responsibility as Home Ministers to make BIMSTEC a model of inclusive development and security

We are committed for full implementation of BIMSTEC Convention on cooperation in combating challenges such as international terrorism, transnational organized crime, and illicit drug trafficking

India has the policy of zero tolerance against terrorism

Our shared resolve must be to ensure that no part of the region provides any scope for terrorist networks to seek shelter, recruit members, undergo training, raise funds, or carry out activities against neighbouring countries

Union Home Minister highlighted the importance of five key areas of cooperation: drug control, counterterrorism and legal cooperation, the repatriation of fugitive criminals, cyber-security and cybercrime investigation, and institutional cooperation and capacity building

Drug trafficking is a form of ‘death trafficking’, there is nothing ‘golden’ about drug trafficking

This is not merely a drug trade; it is an attack on the lives of our youth, our society, our culture, and the future of our coming generations

To tackle the drug menace, we must adopt a “Whole-of-Region” approach

The security of one member country strengthens the security of the entire region, guided by this principle, India remains committed to a peaceful, secure, and prosperous Bay of Bengal region
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                13 OCT 2026 6:44PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Under the
chairmanship
of Union Home Minister Shri Amit Shah, India hosted the first meeting of BIMSTEC Home Ministers in New Delhi, today. The meeting reaffirmed the shared commitment of BIMSTEC member countries to strengthening regional security, trust, and cooperation in the Bay of Bengal region.
In his address, Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation, Shri Amit Shah said that it is a matter of immense pride and privilege for India to host the first BIMSTEC Home Ministers' Meeting. He said BIMSTEC has become an essential platform for regional integration, economic cooperation, and collective security. Under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, India is moving forward with the spirit of ‘
Vishwamitra’
and has always remained committed to peace, coexistence, and human welfare.
Shri Amit Shah said, Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi stated during the 6th BIMSTEC Summit in Bangkok on April 4, 2025, "For us, BIMSTEC is not just a regional organization. It is a model for our inclusive development and security." Shri Shah said, carrying this vision forward, it is our responsibility today as Home Ministers to translate our cooperation into practical mechanisms that strengthen the safety of our citizens and the capabilities of our agencies.
Union Home Minister emphasized India's policy of 'Zero Tolerance' towards terrorism and called for enhanced cooperation in combating terrorism, cross-border organized crime, drug trafficking, human trafficking, and emerging cyber threats. He stressed the importance of timely intelligence sharing, financial investigations, mutual legal assistance, and extradition to ensure that criminals and terrorists are brought to justice. Union Home Minister stated that our shared resolve should be to ensure that terrorist networks are not allowed to find safe havens, recruit members, provide training, raise funds, or carry out activities against neighboring countries from any part of the region. Shri Amit Shah said that, in accordance with national laws and applicable treaties, cooperation in mutual legal assistance and extradition could strengthen our efforts to bring criminals to justice.
Home Minister highlighted the importance of five key areas of cooperation: drug control, counter-terrorism and legal cooperation, repatriation of fugitive criminals, cyber-security and cybercrime investigations, and institutional cooperation and capacity building. He emphasized the need for a coordinated regional approach to combat illicit financial transactions and terror financing. He also stressed the importance of strengthening cooperation among law enforcement agencies, intelligence agencies, and border management agencies.
Shri Amit Shah said, India believes that drug trafficking is essentially 'death trafficking.' In this spirit, he reiterated that there is nothing 'golden' about the trafficking of narcotics. He said, this is not merely the drug trade, but an attack on the lives of our youth, society, culture, and the future of coming generations. Union Home Minister said, this cannot be tackled by the efforts of a single country alone. We must adopt a 'Whole of Region' approach. Shri Shah said, illicit proceeds from drugs provide financial power to organized crime and can also be utilized for terror financing.
He said
the diversion of precursor chemicals and transactions conducted via the dark web further complicate this challenge.
Union Home Minister Shri Amit Shah said that cooperation in disaster management across the BIMSTEC region is one of his highest priorities. He recalled that, during the 6th BIMSTEC Summit, Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi had proposed the establishment of a “BIMSTEC Disaster Management Centre” in India. Shri Shah expressed his pleasure in noting that this centre is planned to be established in Jamnagar, Gujarat. This initiative underscores India's exemplary role as a 'first responder' in the field of disaster management across the entire region. He urged the member countries to actively participate in making the proposed centre operational.
Shri Amit Shah said, the security of one member state strengthens the security of the entire region. He said, India is committed to enhancing trust, respect, and cooperation with all member states for a peaceful, secure, and prosperous Bay of Bengal region, and to achieving concrete outcomes from this meeting.
Union Home Minister of India led the Indian delegation at the Meeting of BIMSTEC Home Ministers, while the Union Home Secretary led the meeting of senior officials. The delegations of all BIMSTEC member states—Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka, and Thailand—participated in the meeting.
The first Meeting of BIMSTEC Home Ministers, held following the meeting of senior officials, provided a valuable opportunity to review the various initiatives undertaken by BIMSTEC in the security sector and to formulate a future course of action to further strengthen regional cooperation in addressing emerging security threats.
Home Ministers of BIMSTEC member countries approved the following:
BIMSTEC Convention against Trafficking in Persons, aimed at enhancing cooperation among member countries in the prevention of human trafficking, criminalization of the offence, and the protection and rehabilitation of victims of human trafficking.
BIMSTEC Plan of Action on Drug Control, aimed at combating the illicit trafficking of narcotic drugs, psychotropic substances, and precursor chemicals.
Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on Capacity Building among BIMSTEC Countries to Combat Money Laundering and Terror Financing, which provides for the training of experts, the exchange of best practices, and extensive cooperation in the areas of financial crimes, financial intelligence, investigations, asset recovery, anti-money laundering measures, countering the financing of terrorism, and countering proliferation financing.
BIMSTEC Plan of Action on Illicit Financial Flows and Their Prevention, aimed at identifying the sources, risks, and channels of illicit financial flows among BIMSTEC member countries.
A Plan of Action for Enhancing Preparedness and Coordination to Address Natural Disasters in the Bay of Bengal Region, proposing coordinated efforts by member countries in regional risk planning, joint exercises, early warning systems, disaster mapping, training centres, information sharing, research, technological innovation, and tsunami risk reduction.
The First Meeting of BIMSTEC Home Ministers also adopted the Delhi Declaration, which outlines various principles guiding security cooperation under BIMSTEC. In the Delhi Declaration adopted at the First BIMSTEC Home Ministers’ Meeting, member countries reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation for regional peace, security, and development. The declaration emphasized combating cross-border terrorism, terror financing, radicalization, drug trafficking, human trafficking, cybercrime, and organized crime. It prioritized information sharing, mutual legal assistance, extradition, capacity building, and the effective implementation of existing agreements and plans of action. It also emphasized the protection of victims of human trafficking involved in online scams. The declaration appreciated India's leadership in strengthening regional security cooperation.
India reiterated its commitment to sharing its expertise in police training, counter-terrorism operations, and forensic investigations. The meeting also emphasized cooperation in disaster management, including the proposed BIMSTEC Centre for Disaster Management in Jamnagar, Gujarat.
This meeting was an important step towards making the BIMSTEC region safer and more prosperous.
The Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC) serves as a vital institutional link between the sub-regions of South and Southeast Asia, promoting multidimensional cooperation, collective security, and economic partnerships among Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka, and Thailand.
During the Fourth BIMSTEC Summit held in 2018, it was decided to convene meetings at the level of BIMSTEC Home Ministers to strengthen cooperation and coordination. Taking an important step towards further consolidating regional security cooperation, Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi extended India's full support to this initiative during the Sixth BIMSTEC Summit and expressed India's commitment to hosting the First Meeting of BIMSTEC Home Ministers.

title: Industrial Pollution Abatement: Sustainability through Regulations under Namami Gange
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                13 OCT 2026 12:44PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Industrial pollution abatement is emerging as a key pillar river rejuvenation, with regulation increasingly evolving from conventional enforcement to continuous compliances, scientific monitoring, cleaner production, resource efficiency and technological improvement.
Under Namami Gange Programme, industrial pollution control has been strengthened through systematic inventorisation and annual inspection of Grossly Polluting Industries (GPIs), independent technical assessments, implementing sector-specific Charters, monitoring of Common Effluent Treatment Plants (CETPs), targeted action plans and sustained regulatory follow-up. Together, these interventions are creating a more accountable and sustainable pathway for industries to reduce pollution while improving water and resource efficiency.
From periodic inspection to continuous compliance
A major intervention has been the establishment of an Annual Inspection mechanism for GPIs, which commenced in 2017 with support of CPCB, the National Regulatory Authority. The programme focusses on 100% inspection of GPIs in the Ganga basin, through third party agencies e.g., technical institutes of national importance and online submission of inspection reports through mobile applications/web portals to enhance efficacy and transparency. For the 2026 inspection cycle, 40 technical institutes have been nominated to participate in the inspection process.
The scale of this monitoring framework has expanded considerably since 2017. In the 2025 inspection cycle, 3,703 GPIs were assessed (1,296 GPIs in the Ganga basin and 2,407 GPIs in the Yamuna basin). The exercise covered 113 districts across six States and one Union Territory, with the GPIs having potential to discharge into 46 tributaries and sub-tributaries of the Ganga and Yamuna.
The inspections go beyond visual assessment. The prescribed methodology includes studying the compliance of the industries against ‘Consent to Operate’ issued by State regulators (State Pollution Control Board) to the individual Industries, sampling from ETP inlets, outlets and aeration tanks, assessment of flow, pH, BOD, COD, TSS and TDS, verification of OCEMS connectivity, examination of recipient drains and water bodies, groundwater assessment, checks for any bypasses and ZLD profiling wherever applicable. Cases involving bypasses, multiple discharge points or defunct/non-existent/non-operational ETPs/ GPIs are reported with geo-tagged photographic or videographic evidence in the portal itself.
Regulation delivering measurable results
The progressive assessment of GPIs demonstrates the impact of sustained regulatory intervention. Across the assessed GPIs, compliance increased from 39% in 2017 to 70% in 2025, while the number of operational GPIs stood at 3,154 in 2025 increasing from 888 in 2017. During the same period, BOD load declined from 26 TPD (2017) to 12.02 TPD (2025), reflecting a substantial reduction in pollution load.
The Ganga basin has exhibited a progressive trend from 2017 to 2025, with compliance rising from 39% in 2017 to 86% in 2025. BOD load declined from 26 TPD to 7.16 TPD, representing a 72.46% reduction, while effluent discharge declined from 349 MLD to 274.88 MLD, a reduction of 21.24%.
The GPI Inspection further recorded that, among 3,145 operational GPIs, 2,715 were compliant, while non-compliant operational GPIs stood at 448, accounting for approximately 14% of operational GPIs. The regulatory process for non-compliant GPIs includes issuance of Show Cause Notices and closure action by State regulators (SPCBs), as applicable.
Thus, regulation is functioning not merely as an enforcement mechanism, but as a continuous self-improvement mechanism—inspection, identification, corrective action and follow-up.
Independent Technical Institutions: adding scientific rigour
A distinctive feature is the involvement of independent technical institutions in industrial inspections. The 2025 exercise engaged 25 technical institutes, while 40 institutes have been nominated for the 2026 cycle. The prescribed inspection team includes at least two experts from a technical institute, a SPCB officer alongwith the participation from State Mission for Clean Ganga/District Ganga Committees.
This model brings guidance from scientific and sector-specific expertise into regulatory oversight for technological or processes improvement in GPIs for pollution and resources reduction with overall improvement in efficiency and compliance to the norms. It also enables inspection findings to be supported by laboratory analysis, OCEMS verification, field observations and geo-tagged evidence, thereby strengthening the credibility and effectiveness of compliance assessment.
Sector-specific Charters: from pollution control to pollution prevention
The regulatory framework has also expanded upstream - from treating pollution after it is generated to preventing pollution at source. Sector-specific Charters have been developed for Pulp & Paper, Sugar, Distillery, Textile and Tannery sectors. These five sectors collectively represented around 70% of GPIs in the Ganga basin and 88% of the total pollution load in the earlier assessment.
The Charter for Water Recycling and Pollution Prevention Industries specifically seeks to optimise water and chemical use, reduce freshwater consumption and wastewater generation, improve effluent treatment and promote reuse and recycling, with the ultimate objective of preventing discharge of untreated effluent into recipient river streams.
The Charter establishes measurable targets, including reduction in water consumption, ETP/RO upgradation and, in the longer term, recycling of water against total input. It also explicitly envisages third-party involvement in planning, assessment, design and monitoring of process technologies and ETP upgradation, bringing regulators, technical institutions, research organisations and industry stakeholders together.
Targeted action for high pollution-load industries
Targeted interventions have also been undertaken for industries contributing significantly to pollution load. In 2022, 246 GPIs were identified as top contributors requiring priority action. To address their pollution load, 17 sector-specific workshops were conducted, with 222 GPIs participating and submitting action plans. The remaining 24 GPIs were either closed or had shifted to dry operations.
The progress of these industries was assessed against short-, medium- and long-term goals. 173 GPIs achieved short-term goals, 141 achieved medium-term goals and 126 achieved long-term goals. An estimated 65% reduction in pollution load was recorded during 2022–23 compared with 2021–22, with the pollution load declining from 18.68 TPD to 6.381 TPD. Subsequently, 156 industries came out of the priority list, while 66 remained for priority action
CETPs: strengthening pollution control at industrial clusters
Industrial clusters often require a collective approach to effluent treatment. Common Effluent Treatment Plants (CETPs) provide a shared treatment facility for industries located within such clusters, enabling their wastewater to be treated collectively. CETPs therefore form an important component of industrial pollution abatement, particularly in industrial clusters.
In 2025, 41 CETPs were assessed across the Ganga and Yamuna main-stem States, of which 40 were operational. Their combined operational capacity stood at 514.53 MLD, with utilisation of 286.31 MLD, while 27 CETPs were complying with the prescribed requirements. The assessment also identified specific operational and technological gaps and enabled measures such as improvement in operation and maintenance, upgradation of treatment systems, introduction of biological treatment where required, improved functioning of Primary Effluent Treatment Plants and regular monitoring of outlet quality.
The assessment of CETPs has enabled specific interventions rather than one-size-fits-all approach. Measures include improvement in operation and maintenance, upgradation of treatment systems, introduction of biological treatment where required, improved operation of Primary Effluent Treatment Plants, regular outlet monitoring and cleaner chemical practices.
For textile clusters, recommended measures include adoption of a Chemical Management System, eco-friendly non-toxic chemicals and low-salt dyes. For tannery clusters, cleaner production measures, improved PETP treatment and mechanical desalting have been recommended.
Water conservation: turning treated wastewater into a resource
One of the important shifts has been the recognition of treated wastewater as a resource rather than merely a waste stream.
The Charter-based interventions have helped industries reduce specific freshwater consumption and wastewater generation through reuse and recycling. The latest assessment records substantial reductions across major sectors, alongside increased adoption of treatment and recycling technologies.
The Sugar sector, for instance, has witnessed a major improvement in resource efficiency. Between 2017 and 2025, freshwater consumption declined from 155 L/T cane to 58 L/T cane, wastewater discharge declined from 190 L/T cane to 136 L/T cane, and BOD discharge declined from 0.0065 kg/T cane to 0.0029 kg/T cane. The improvement has been supported by high-pressure boilers, Condensate Polishing Units, tertiary ETP upgradation, reuse of treated wastewater and other process improvements.
The Pulp & Paper sector has also recorded significant resource-efficiency gains. The latest assessment reports 60 recycled-fibre-based Pulp & Paper mills operating on Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD), along with estimated savings of 928.89 MLD of groundwater and corresponding energy conservation of 1,649.80 MW annually.
Present CETPs in industrial clusters of Ganga basin are designed with an approach of reuse of treated water by the member industrial units.
A new paradigm of sustainable industrial regulation
The impact of industrial pollution-control measures is reflected not only in compliance statistics but also in broader environmental outcomes.
The assessment records no black liquor discharge from Pulp & Paper mills, no effluent discharge from distilleries, no incidence of coloured water discharge and fish mortality, approximately 719 million litres of groundwater saved per day, and improved water quality in tributaries including Ramganga, Kosi, Dhela and Bahela.
The interventions have also contributed to around 1,277.6 MW/year of energy savings and an estimated 1,162.6 tonnes CO₂e reduction in carbon footprint.
Sustaining pollution abatement through regulation
The industrial pollution abatement journey under Namami Gange reflects an important evolution in environmental governance leading to the efficient compliance achievement.
The approach combines regulation with science, enforcement with facilitation, monitoring with technology and compliance with resource efficiency. Annual GPI inspections provide the regulatory backbone; independent technical institutions add scientific rigour; sector-specific Charters encourage cleaner production and water recycling; targeted action plans address high pollution-load industries; and CETP assessments strengthen pollution control at industrial clusters.
The numbers tell the story. In the 2025 assessment, 3,703 GPIs were covered, including 1,296 in the Ganga basin and 2,407 in the Yamuna basin. The Ganga basin has seen compliance rise from 39% in 2017 to 86% in 2025, alongside a 72.46% reduction in BOD load.
The objective is therefore no longer limited to ensuring that industries comply with prescribed norms. It is about creating an enduring culture of responsible production, water conservation, pollution prevention, reuse and recycling.
From regulation to responsibility, from monitoring to measurable outcomes, and from pollution control to sustainable production, industrial pollution abatement is becoming a sustained and integral part of the journey towards cleaner and healthier rivers.

title: Retrospective regularization of exempt status of Provident Fund (PF) Trusts through Amnesty Scheme, 2026
subtitle: EPFO steps up nationwide drive and reminds eligible establishments as deadline of 28 December approaches
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                13 OCT 2026 2:37PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Provisions for Amnesty were introduced as a transitional measure in the Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF) Scheme 2026, notified on 29.06.2026. These provisions offer a one-time opportunity for regularisation of exemption status of Provident Fund (PF) Trusts that are recognized under the Income Tax Act, 1961 (43 of 1961), but lack a formal exemption order granted under section 17 of the Employees’ Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions (EPF&MP) Act, 1952 or section 143 of the Code on Social Security (CoSS), 2020.
The operational guidelines for Amnesty, including the manner of application and procedural requirements, were detailed in the circular issued on 11.07.2026. The Amnesty window remains open for a period of six (6) months from the date of notification, expiring on 28.12.2026. With less than three months remaining before the deadline, the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) is urging eligible establishments pan-India to expedite their submissions. Besides retrospective regularisation of exempt status, key benefits under the scheme include waivers of statutory requirements under the CoSS, 2020—such as minimum employee headcount, corpus size, and the 3-year compliance rule—along with complete operational flexibility postregularisation to comply either as an exempt or an unexempt establishment.
To ensure maximum awareness, EPFO has rolled out extensive multi-channel initiatives across the country. Strategic meetings and seminars have been conducted in collaboration with apex industry and market bodies, including the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), and the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE). Chartered Accountants and statutory auditors have been specifically engaged to identify and assist qualifying PF Trusts. In parallel, EPFO Zonal and Regional Offices pan-India have organized nationwide seminars and workshops to engage directly with local establishments, employers, and trust members, supported by multi-media campaigns, social media outreach, and explanatory infographics simplifying procedural compliance guidelines.
To support applicants effectively, the Exemption Division (Head Office) has conducted dedicated hybrid training programs for EPFO field officials posted across the country. In addition, dual-track institutional and employer training has been carried out both through online modules and physically at the Pandit Deendayal Upadhyaya National Academy of Social Security (PDUNASS) for departmental officers and employers alike.
Furthermore, EPFO has actively coordinated with the Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue / Income Tax Department) to institutionalize data sharing of exempted establishment records. This data integration focuses on identifying, cross-verifying, and bringing unnotified or non-compliant PF trusts under the statutory umbrella, while ensuring that tax-recognized trusts without formal EPFO exemption orders regularize their status promptly. EPFO Regional Offices nationwide continue active follow-ups to facilitate the submission of regularisation applications within the stipulated timeframe.
Eligible PF Trusts across India are advised to avail of this one-time opportunity to enable continuance of income tax benefits available to trusts recognized by the Income tax department.

date:

content:
The Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice, is observing the “Special Campaign 6” and organised a workshop on “Record Management” on 13th October, 2026, at the Conference Hall, Kartavya Bhawan 2, New Delhi, under the guidance of the Secretary, Legislative Department, Dr. Rajiv Mani.
The workshop was led by Shri G. Panmei, JS&LC, Legislative Department, and attended by officers and staff members of the Department, including those from its attached offices, namely, the Official Languages Wing and Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan.
Shri Ranjan Kumar, former Faculty Member, Institute of Secretariat Training and Management, New Delhi, was present at the workshop as the Resource Person and shared his valuable insights on record management. During the workshop, Shri Ranjan Kumar, highlighted the significance of effective record management in promoting administrative efficiency, transparency and accountability. He emphasised the need for systematic maintenance of official records, proper classification and indexing of files and documents, timely review of records, and their preservation or weeding out in accordance with the prescribed rules and guidelines. He further underscored the importance of adhering to record retention schedules and ensuring the proper disposal of records in accordance with the applicable procedures.
Shri G. Panmei, JS&LC, expressed his sincere gratitude to Shri Ranjan Kumar, for sharing his valuable insights and expertise on record management. He also encouraged the officers and employees to ensure the systematic maintenance and proper preservation of official records, their timely review, and adherence to the prescribed rules and guidelines regarding record retention and weeding out. He emphasised that effective record management is essential for the smooth functioning of the Department and for enhancing administrative efficiency and accountability.

title: Ministry of Mines Organises Outreach Programme on Auction of Offshore Mineral Blocks
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                13 OCT 2026 8:11PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Mines, Government of India, organised an Outreach Programme on Auction of Offshore Mineral Blocks on 13th October 2026 at New Delhi. The programme provided a platform for prospective bidders and stakeholders to understand the two offshore mineral blocks offered for auction, the applicable policy and regulatory framework, the bidding process and the support available for exploration.
The Ministry has issued the Notice Inviting Tender (NIT) dated 1 October 2026 for the grant of operating rights for two offshore mineral blocks,
Sewell Rise-01 and West Sewell Ridge-01
, located in the Andaman Sea. Both blocks contain polymetallic nodules and crusts and are being offered for the grant of a Composite Licence. Sewell Rise-01 covers an area of 632 square kilometres, while West Sewell Ridge-01 covers 1,000 square kilometres, taking the total area offered for auction to 1,632 square kilometres.
Shri Keshav Chandra, Secretary, Ministry of Mines,
highlighted the importance of strengthening India’s mineral supply chains to support economic growth, technological advancement, the energy transition and manufacturing competitiveness. He highlighted the potential of the Critical Mineral Processing Park coming up on the eastern coast of India to support offshore mineral processing.
Dr. Veena Kumari Dermal, Additional Secretary, Ministry of Mines,
highlighted the policy reforms undertaken to facilitate the transparent and responsible development of India’s offshore mineral resources. Taking stakeholder feedback into account, the Ministry has revised block configurations, including increasing the area of polymetallic nodule and crust blocks to provide greater operational flexibility for offshore exploration. She also noted that the Terms of Reference and Guidelines for Baseline Environmental Data Collection and Environmental Management Plans for offshore mineral exploration and exploitation in India’s Exclusive Economic Zone have been circulated to the concerned Central Ministries and Departments for comments and will be finalised shortly.
The Geological Survey of India (GSI) presented an overview of the offshore mineral blocks, including their geological characteristics and mineral potential. SBI Capital Markets Limited (SBICAPS), the Transaction Advisor, explained the policy framework, auction process, tender provisions and bidding requirements. MSTC, the auction platform provider, demonstrated the step-by-step procedure for purchasing tender documents and submitting bids through the e-auction portal.
The National Mineral Exploration and Development Trust (NMEDT) presented the scheme for partial reimbursement of exploration expenses for Composite Licence holders of offshore mineral blocks. The presentation outlined the support available to facilitate exploration activities.
An open-house discussion enabled participants to interact with the Ministry and the organisations involved in the auction. Prospective bidders and other stakeholders sought clarifications and shared their views on the blocks, tender conditions, auction procedures and exploration-related support.
The auction is being conducted under the Offshore Areas Mineral (Development and Regulation) Act, 2002, as amended in 2023, and the Offshore Areas Mineral (Auction) Rules, 2024, as amended. The auction framework seeks to ensure transparency in the allocation of offshore mineral resources and facilitate systematic exploration and responsible development of India’s offshore mineral potential.
Polymetallic nodules and crusts contain minerals such as nickel, cobalt, copper and manganese, which are important for various industrial applications and emerging technologies. The initiative forms part of the Government of India’s efforts to advance offshore mineral exploration and strengthen the country’s mineral resource base. Systematic exploration will be essential to establish the mineral potential of the blocks and assess their prospects for future development.
Auction Schedule
The sale of tender documents commenced on 1 October 2026. The pre-bid conference is scheduled for 4 November 2026, and the last date for submission of queries is 13 November 2026. Tender documents may be purchased up to 21 December 2026, while the last date for submission of bids is 28 December 2026.
The Notice Inviting Tender and related auction documents are available on the MSTC e-auction portal:
https://www.mstcecommerce.com/auctionhome/mlcln/index.jsp

title: Ministry of Panchayati Raj to undertake cleanliness drive and disposal of pending matters on 14 October 2026 under Special Campaign 6.0
subtitle: Panchayati Raj Institutions and Rural Local Bodies across States and Union Territories to Participate in a Dedicated One-Day Drive for Cleanliness, Improved Public Spaces and Expedited Disposal of Pending Matters
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                13 OCT 2026 6:16PM by PIB Delhi
content:
As part of the ongoing Special Campaign 6.0 for Institutionalising Swachhata and Minimising Pendency (SCDPM 6.0), the Ministry of Panchayati Raj (MoPR) will organise a dedicated one-day cleanliness and pendency disposal drive on 14 October 2026. The drive is part of the Implementation Phase of the Campaign, being observed from 2 October to 31 October 2026. It aims to promote workplace cleanliness, improve the use of office space and expedite the disposal of pending matters, including references and other identified pendencies. Activities planned for the day include cleanliness shramdaan and Swachhata drives at workplaces and workstations, minor repairs and removal of clutter, staff orientation on bio-waste management, proper collection, segregation and disposal of e-waste, scrap disposal, public grievance redressal, interaction with Safai Mitras and review of progress under the Campaign. All Divisions and Sections of the Ministry are actively participating in the Campaign and taking steps to ensure the timely completion of planned activities.
To encourage grassroots-level participation, 14 October 2026 has also been designated for Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)/Rural Local Bodies (RLBs) across the country to undertake dedicated campaign activities. The Ministry had earlier issued an advisory on 12 October 2026 to the Additional Chief Secretaries, Principal Secretaries and Secretaries of the Panchayati Raj Departments of all States and Union Territories, calling for the active participation of PRIs/RLBs. The activities will include cleanliness drives in Panchayat offices and nearby public places, removal of unused materials, beautification of public spaces using locally available resources and tree plantation with community participation. PRIs will also review pending complaints, grievances and applications for timely disposal. Personnel engaged in cleanliness and sanitation activities will be felicitated.
As part of its efforts to improve workplace efficiency, the Ministry also organised an e-Office training session for its officials and staff at Jeevan Prakash Building, New Delhi. The session covered the latest e-Office features, file workflow processes and digital record management, with a focus on smoother file movement and timely disposal of official work. These initiatives seek to promote Swachhata, minimise pendency and strengthen efficient, accountable and responsive governance in line with the objectives of Special Campaign 6.0.

title: DARPG releases the 53rd Monthly Report on Centralized Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS) for Central Ministries/ Departments performance for the month of September, 2026
subtitle:
A total of 2,38,579 grievances redressed by Central Ministries/ Departments in September, 2026.

For the 51st month in a row, the monthly disposal crossed 1 lakh cases in the Central Secretariat

Department of Posts, Department of Financial Services (Insurance Division) & Department of Telecommunications top the Group A category in the GRAI rankings released for the month of September, 2026

Ministry of Textiles, Ministry of Heavy Industries & Ministry of Tourism top in Group B category in the GRAI rankings released for the month of September, 2026
ministry: Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                13 OCT 2026 12:43PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG) released the Centralized Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS) monthly report for September, 2026, which provides a detailed analysis of types and categories of public grievances and the nature of disposal. This is the 53rd report on Central Ministries/Departments published by DARPG.
The progress for September, 2026 indicates 2,38,579 Grievances redressed by Central Ministries/Departments. The Average Grievance Disposal Time in the Central Ministries/Departments for 2026 is 13 days. These reports are part of the 10-step CPGRAMS reform process which was adopted by DARPG to improve the quality of disposal and reduce the timelines.
The report provides the data for new users registered through the CPGRAMS Portal in the month of September, 2026. title: From Farms to Borders: NH-22 Four-Laning Project to Boost Connectivity and Economic Growth in Bihar
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                13 OCT 2026 4:25PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Road infrastructure plays a vital role in connecting agricultural regions, industrial centres and border areas with wider markets. In Bihar, the Muzaffarpur–Sitamarhi–Sonbarsa section of National Highway-22 (NH-22) serves as an important link between a major economic centre and the India–Nepal border. Its upgradation to four lanes will enhance the capacity of this corridor and strengthen regional connectivity.
The project is expected to facilitate smoother movement of passengers and freight, improve access to economic centres and support regional trade. It will also strengthen links between road, rail and other logistics infrastructure, creating a more integrated transport network for North Bihar.
In August 2026, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) approved the upgradation of this 82.57-km section to four lanes at a total capital cost of ₹3,590.73 crore under the Hybrid Annuity Mode (HAM).
Strengthening Connectivity to the Nepal Border
NH-22 connects Muzaffarpur with Sonbarsa on the India–Nepal border. At Muzaffarpur, it intersects NH-27, which forms part of the East-West Corridor. Towards Sonbarsa, the highway provides an important link between the national highway network and cross-border transport infrastructure.
The upgraded corridor will support cross-border passenger and cargo movement through the nearby Bhithamore Land Port. By improving connectivity between economic centres and border areas, it is expected to facilitate regional trade and enhance the efficiency of goods movement.
Four-Laning for Smoother and Safer Travel
The existing route passes through densely populated areas, including Muzaffarpur, Muksudpur, Runni Saidpur, Thumma, Dumra, Bhutahi and Sonbarsa. Four-laning is expected to ease congestion along these stretches and improve traffic flow.
Designed for a speed of 100 kmph, with an average operating speed of 80 kmph and no at-grade median openings, the upgraded highway will support more predictable journeys for passenger and freight traffic.
The project includes seven major bridges, including a 340-metre bridge over the perennial Bagmati River, three railway overbridges and two flyovers. These structures will address key crossing points, improve traffic continuity and help reduce conflicts between road and railway movement.
Integrating Industry, Railways and Logistics
Planned under the PM GatiShakti National Master Plan, the project aims to strengthen connectivity between industrial centres, agricultural production areas and logistics infrastructure.
The corridor will connect five economic nodes, including four industrial estates and a Mega Food Park, supporting manufacturing, food processing and agro-based industries. Improved access to Muzaffarpur and Sitamarhi railway stations will also facilitate multimodal logistics and freight movement.
Its links with NH-31 and NH-122 will further integrate the corridor with Bihar's transport network. Enhanced connectivity towards Barauni's industrial hub and riverine logistics centres along the Ganga is expected to create opportunities for inland waterway trade and improve supply-chain efficiency.
Strengthening Farm-to-Market Links
For a region where agriculture is an important part of the local economy, improved road connectivity can make the movement of produce to markets and processing centres more efficient. Reduced travel time, lower transportation costs and improved fuel efficiency are expected to support more reliable supply chains.
Better connections with railway stations, industrial estates and wider transport corridors will also facilitate the movement of agricultural produce to markets beyond the immediate region.
Improving Access to Key Destinations
The upgraded highway will improve access to important religious, cultural and social destinations, including Baba Garibnath Temple, Mata Janki Temple, Punaura Dham and the Buddhist Circuit.
It will also strengthen connectivity to Muzaffarpur and Sitamarhi, both identified as aspirational districts, supporting regional mobility and access to important destinations.
Building a More Integrated Transport Network
The four-laning of NH-22 will strengthen a key corridor linking economic centres, agricultural areas, industrial nodes and the India–Nepal border. With improved highway capacity, upgraded crossing infrastructure and stronger links to railways and logistics facilities, the project is designed to address existing traffic constraints while supporting the region's connectivity needs.
By bringing together road transport, industrial activity, agricultural supply chains and cross-border movement, the Muzaffarpur–Sitamarhi–Sonbarsa corridor will contribute to a more integrated transport network in the region, boosting connectivity and economic activity.

title: Preserving Himalayas a National Responsibility; Every Citizen Has a Stake: Dr Jitendra Singh
subtitle:
Himalayan ecosystem sustains springs, water bodies and river sources while supporting tourism, agriculture and livelihoods, says Dr. Jitendra Singh

Union Minister stresses balance between development needs and ecological safeguards, cautioning against unauthorised construction and unregulated activities

Ministry of Science & Technology initiatives include Himalayan ecosystem research centres, glacier monitoring, glaciology training and climate change research: Dr. Jitendra Singh

Aroma Mission and Purple Revolution gave J&K national identity, demonstrate how science and market linkages can create livelihood opportunities: Dr. Jitendra Singh

date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                13 OCT 2026 5:03PM by PIB Jammu and Kashmir
content:
Preserving the Himalayas and the Himalayan ecosystem is a national responsibility because every citizen has a stake in protecting this vital natural resource, Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science and Technology and Earth Sciences, Dr. Jitendra Singh, said on Tuesday. He emphasised that the responsibility for safeguarding the Himalayan region extends beyond the government and scientific community to every citizen.
The special session, held at the Shalimar Convention Centre of Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology of Kashmir (SKUAST-K), was part of the 13th All India Sustainable Mountain Development Summit, being held from October 12 to 14 under the theme “Contouring Sustainable Himalayan Landscapes for Inclusive Viksit Bharat”. The summit is jointly organised by SKUAST-K and the Integrated Mountain Initiative (IMI), with deliberations centred on sustainable mountain development and the draft Jammu & Kashmir Sustainable Mountain Development Policy 2026.
Those present included Secretary, Science and Technology, Babila Rakwal, Vice-Chancellor of SKUAST-K Prof. Nazir A. Ganai, and representatives of academia and the mountain development community.
Addressing the special session, the Minister said Himalayas are crucial to the country’s ecological security and support springs, water bodies, river sources and glaciers. The region also sustains tourism, agriculture and livelihoods, making its protection essential for both environmental security and inclusive economic development.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said the challenge is to balance development requirements and livelihood opportunities with the need to preserve a fragile mountain ecosystem. Unauthorised construction, unregulated activities and other human-made lap can aggravate risks in sensitive mountain regions. Ecological safeguards, therefore, must remain integral to development planning, supported by responsible public conduct and greater awareness among local communities and other stakeholders.
The Minister referred to the Department of Science and Technology (DST) Ministry of Science & Technology work under the National Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem, part of the National Action Plan on Climate Change. DST has identified three centres at the University of Kashmir, Sikkim University and Tezpur University to strengthen research on climate change and the Himalayan ecosystem. Climate change research and institutional capacity-building are also being supported through state-level initiatives across the Indian Himalayan Region.
He cited glacier monitoring and field-based research undertaken by the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology in Ladakh and the Doda region since 2015. The work includes the use of automatic weather stations and seismometers, along with studies relating to landslides and past earthquakes. The Minister also referred to capacity-building in glaciology in Kashmir as part of efforts to strengthen scientific expertise and understanding of the region’s changing environment.
Referring to improvements in weather observation, Dr. Jitendra Singh said India’s weather radar network had expanded from 16 radars in 2014 to 50, with another 50 planned under Mission Mausam. Such scientific infrastructure strengthens weather monitoring and preparedness, particularly in regions exposed to extreme weather and natural hazards.
The Minister also referred to a pilot study initiated by the Wadia Institute in 10 villages in Jammu and Kashmir. The findings could help inform locally appropriate measures and guide the possible replication of suitable interventions. He asked that the draft Jammu and Kashmir Sustainable Mountain Development Policy be examined in this context.
Dr. Jitendra Singh cited the Aroma Mission and the Purple Revolution as examples of science-led livelihood generation in Jammu and Kashmir. Lavender cultivation in areas such as Gulmarg and Padder has created opportunities for farmers and rural entrepreneurs, demonstrating the potential of region-specific crops to support local economic activity.
He stressed that such initiatives require more than cultivation alone. Strong market linkages connecting growers with aroma and fragrance industries, access to technology and finance, and support for entrepreneurship are essential to make these opportunities sustainable. Women’s self-help groups and young entrepreneurs can also play an important role in expanding livelihood opportunities. The experience of Jammu and Kashmir offers lessons for other regions seeking to build local economies around their natural and agricultural strengths.
Reiterating the need for collective action, the Minister said that scientific interventions and government programmes must be complemented by responsible decisions on the ground. Protecting the Himalayas is essential not only for the region’s communities and livelihoods but also for the long-term ecological well-being of the country.

title: New technology provides environment friendly route for treating dye-contaminated wastewater
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                13 OCT 2026 3:09PM by PIB Delhi
content:
A sustainable, multifunctional machine learning enabled filter for wastewater treatment, developed by integrating green-synthesized zinc oxide (ZnO) nanoparticles with biodegradable polylactic acid (PLA) nanofibers, assisted by machine learning can provide an environment friendly route for treating dye-contaminated wastewater.
The discharge of persistent organic dyes from industrial activities, particularly the textile industry, represents an important environmental challenge because these compounds can be stable, toxic, and resistant to natural degradation. The research addresses the need for sustainable wastewater-treatment technologies.
Existing wastewater-treatment approaches such as adsorption, sedimentation and flocculation can separate pollutants but do not necessarily destroy them. Biological treatment can also be slow for highly stable dyes. Photocatalysis offers an attractive alternative because it can degrade pollutants under relatively mild conditions while using renewable energy.
However, conventional photocatalytic systems face several challenges: recovery of nanoparticle catalysts; separation of catalysts from treated water; electron-hole recombination; dependence on light availability; and the requirement for efficient catalyst-pollutant contact.
To tackle this challenge, a new technology developed by the Institute of Nano Science and Technology (INST) Mohali, autonomous institute of the Department of Science and Technology (DST) immobilised ZnO (zinc oxide prepared from natural sources) within porous PLA nanofibers and introduced mechanical excitation along with light. The mechanical vibrations generated piezoelectric polarization, which suppressed photogenerated electron–hole recombination and enhanced reactive-species formation. The work was published in the journal Advanced Functional Materials (Wiley).
Fig 1
:
Schematic illustration of green-synthesized, highly crystalline ZnO nanoparticles using turmeric powder.
Dr. Aviru Kumar Basu’s lab synthesised ZnO nanoparticles using turmeric extract, where naturally occurring bioactive compounds like curcumin, flavonoids and phenolic compounds acted as reducing and stabilizing agents, avoiding conventional synthesis routes involving harmful reagents.
The fabrication of PLA-ZnO nanofibers through electrospinning, produced a porous, high-surface-area and mechanically stable catalytic membrane rather than using ZnO as a freely dispersed powder. The integration of photocatalysis and piezocatalysis enabled pollutant degradation using both light and mechanical vibrations.
The PLA-ZnO nanofibers achieved 98.6% MB and 96.7% CR decolorization within 120 min under combined light and ultrasonic excitation. This new material also demonstrated antibacterial activity, achieving approximately 75% inactivation of
E. coli
and 71% of
S. aureus
after 6 h. Machine learning (ML) was integrated with the experimental study to predict dye-decolorization behaviour from parameters such as wavelength, time, catalyst amount, ultrasonic frequency, light intensity and dye concentration.
Fig 2
: Schematic of PLA-ZnO nanofiber preparation using the e-spin method.
The developed PLA-ZnO nanofibers can be used for the treatment of wastewater containing persistent organic dyes and microbial contaminants, particularly those associated with textile and industrial effluents for cleaner and safer water. They can also be used for Photocatalytic and piezocatalytic environmental remediation as well as for antibacterial water-treatment membranes.

MSDC is the cooperative federalism at play in maritime governance, delivering for our ports & for port-led industrialisation: Sarbananda Sonowal
ministry: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                13 OCT 2026 6:53PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The 21st Maritime State Development Council (MSDC) concluded today in Mumbai with landmark outcomes for India’s maritime sector. This was the first meeting of the MSDC after its recognition as a statutory consultative body under the Indian Ports Act, 2025, notified on 15th May 2026. The Council, originally constituted in 1997, now functions with an enhanced mandate to promote integrated maritime growth, coordinated policy formulation, and planned development of maritime infrastructure.
Chaired by
Union Minister for Ports, Shipping & Waterways
,
Shri Sarbananda Sonowal
, the MSDC meeting brought together Ministers of Coastal States, Administrators of Union Territories, senior officials of State Maritime Boards, Chairpersons of Major Ports, allied maritime institutions, and representatives of Central Ministries. Among the dignitaries present were
Shri Kanubhai Desai
, Finance Minister of Gujarat;
Shri Digambar V. Kamat
, Minister (Ports), Government of Goa;
Shri Nitesh Rane
,
Minister of Fisheries & Ports Development, Government of Maharashtra; and
Shri Malladi Krishna Rao
, Minister from Puducherry. Senior Secretaries and CEOs of Maritime Boards from Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, West Bengal, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, and Kerala also participated, along with Chairpersons of Major Ports including Deendayal, JNPA, MbPA, Cochin, Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Paradip, SMPA, Kamarajar, and Mormugao. Heads of allied organisations such as the Inland Waterways Authority of India, Shipping Corporation of India, Dredging Corporation of India, Indian Port Rail & Ropeway Corporation, Cochin Shipyard, Indian Maritime University, DPIIT, NITI Aayog, Indian Navy and Coast Guard were also in attendance.
The meeting was preceded by
educational
port visits to the Mumbai Port Authority Cruise Terminal and Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority (JNPA), showcasing India’s cruise and container port capabilities.
During the deliberations, the Council adopted the Maritime India Vision 2030 and Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 targets, which together identify over 500 initiatives across ports, shipping, inland waterways, shipbuilding, green shipping and global collaboration. States and State Maritime Boards were urged to prepare Port Master Plans for Other Than Major Ports aligned with these national targets, with MoPSW sharing the standardized template used by Major Ports.
The Council endorsed the priorities of the National Perspective Plan and urged States to fast-track multimodal connectivity projects through road, rail, inland waterways, pipelines and conveyors. It resolved that States, in coordination with MoPSW, to develop port-linked industrial clusters with land availability, plug-and-play infrastructure and fast-tracked approvals, integrated with port capacity expansion and connectivity projects.
On statutory compliance, the Council approved draft MSDC Regulations and Guidelines on port data and tariff transparency, and instructed all States and Union Territories to notify subordinate rules under Section 77 of the Act within three months.
"The Indian Ports Act gave the MSD council its legal foundation. Today the Centre and the coastal states turned that foundation into a shared work plan, with deadlines every one of us has agreed to meet," Sarbananda Sonowal said. "This is cooperative federalism in maritime governance, delivering for our ports and for port-led industrialisation."
In a major step towards ease of doing business, the Council resolved that the One Nation One Port Process (ONOP) reforms, including One Nation One Documentation, Port Process Re-engineering and Inter-ministerial Process Reforms, to be implemented across all ports by March 2027. It further resolved that all ports shall integrate with the Maritime Single Window (MSW – Sagar Setu) by March 2027, ensuring unified digital processes nationwide. Transparency of port tariffs through electronic publication was also mandated. To support uniform implementation, Minister
Shri Sarbananda Sonowal
launched the
Ready Reckoner for Implementing ONOP
, a comprehensive guide for Major and Other Than Major Ports. The document includes references to central circulars issued by CBIC, MHA and MoHFW for implementing inter-ministerial process reforms, and sets out clear expectations from State and Union Territory Governments to expedite ONOP implementation.
The Council gave particular emphasis to port connectivity, shipbuilding and cruise shipping. It resolved to prioritise connectivity projects under Sagarmala, implement the National Coastal and Inland Shipping Strategic Plan, promote modal shift of cargo to coastal shipping, facilitate development of shipbuilding, ship-repair and recycling clusters, and leverage the Maritime Development Fund, Shipbuilding Development Scheme and Shipbuilding Financial Assistance Programme for financing. Cruise shipping infrastructure development at Major and Non-Major Ports was also endorsed.
A significant announcement was made by Union Minister
Sarbananda Sonowal
, introducing two specialized credit risk insurance products to support India’s shipbuilding industry under the National Shipbuilding Mission. Developed under the Shipbuilding Development Scheme (SbDS), these first-of-their-kind insurance policies aim to reduce financial stress in large-scale ship manufacturing. The
Shipbuilding Project Credit Risk Insurance Policy (SbPCP)
, developed by ECGC Ltd., will cover export projects, while the
Business Credit Shield Policy–Shipbuilders (BCSPS)
, developed by The New India Assurance Co. Ltd. (NIACL), will protect domestic projects. The Government of India will subsidise insurance premiums and provide direct support to insurers in case shipyards file claims. Speaking on the occasion,
Shri Sonowal
said,
“Building a ship is a massive, multi-year journey, a single missed milestone payment could stall an entire shipyard’s operations. With these new insurance policies, we are stepping in to give them a real safety net. We want our shipyards to focus on what they do best
,
building world-class vessels
,
without the fear of delayed payments or sudden global market shifts holding them back.”
Union Minister
Sarbananda Sonowal
emphasized the significance of the meeting, stating,
“The MSDC has now entered a new statutory phase, strengthening cooperative federalism in maritime governance. With the adoption of MIV 2030 and MAKV 2047 targets, India’s ports and shipping sector will be future-ready, competitive and aligned with global standards. The Council’s resolutions today mark a decisive step towards integrated maritime growth and port-led industrialisation.”
The 21st MSDC has set a jointly owned course of action for integrated development of Major and Non-Major Ports, reinforcing India’s maritime vision under Maritime India Vision 2030 and Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047.
Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal called the meeting "a meeting of Team India" and tied the council's work to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's call of "Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas and Sabka Prayas," or together with all, development for all, trust of all, effort of all.

content:
Through the National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction (NAPDDR), the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment provides support to individuals affected by substance use through treatment, counselling, rehabilitation and social reintegration services.
Access to de-addiction treatment, rehabilitation and sustained psychological support can play an important role in helping individuals overcome substance dependence and rebuild their lives.
Amit Kumar
(name changed),
aged 47, belongs to the Other Backward Classes (OBC) community and resides in Gorakhpur district of Uttar Pradesh. He was engaged in self-employment but faced significant personal, social and economic challenges due to substance addiction. Influenced by bad company and stress, he developed a habit of smoking and using addictive substances. Over time, his addiction adversely affected his physical and mental well-being, reduced his self-confidence and created difficulties in maintaining regular work and healthy social relationships. Coming from a financially disadvantaged family, he experienced economic hardship and an unstable income due to irregular employment. Social stigma further contributed to his isolation, while strained family relationships added to his difficulties.
Despite these challenges, Amit Kumar aspired to overcome his addiction, regain his self-respect, lead a healthier life and support his family financially. He had previously undergone treatment in 2018 and experienced improvement, but subsequently relapsed. Determined to recover and rebuild his life, he sought treatment again and committed himself to the recovery process.
On 13 August 2021, Amit Kumar received support under the National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction (NAPDDR) through Basudev Tiwari Sewa Sansthan’s Punarjanm Integrated Rehabilitation Centre for Addicts (IRCA) in Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh. The centre provided free de-addiction treatment, medical care, prescribed medicines, psychological counselling and motivational support. Regular counselling sessions and follow-up care helped him address the challenges associated with addiction and remain committed to his recovery. Family counselling and emotional support also played an important role in rebuilding his confidence, improving family relationships and supporting his reintegration into society.
With sustained assistance from the centre and his own determination, Amit Kumar successfully quit smoking and substance use. Following his recovery, he resumed working and established a livelihood by driving his own auto-rickshaw. He now earns approximately ₹30,000 per month, a significant improvement from his earlier situation of irregular work and unstable income. His earnings have helped improve his family’s financial condition and enabled him to contribute more consistently towards household expenses. The combination of treatment, counselling, rehabilitation and follow-up support has helped him move towards a healthier, more responsible and financially stable life.
Amit Kumar’s journey highlights the role of the National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction in supporting recovery, rehabilitation and socio-economic reintegration among individuals affected by substance dependence. The assistance provided through Punarjanm IRCA helped him regain his confidence, resume productive work and work towards financial self-reliance. His experience demonstrates how timely treatment, psychological support and family involvement can create opportunities for individuals to overcome addiction, rebuild relationships and lead a dignified life.
Amit Kumar’s transformation from addiction and economic uncertainty to recovery and livelihood security stands as an encouraging example of resilience and renewed hope. His journey reinforces the importance of accessible de-addiction services and sustained rehabilitation support in helping individuals reclaim their lives, strengthen their families and move towards a healthier and more secure future.

title: Strong Statistical Systems Key to Achieving Viksit Bharat @ 2047: Dr. P. K. Mishra
subtitle:

"The Quality of Our Data Influences the Quality of Our Decisions and Development Outcomes”: Principal Secretary to PM

"Statistics Are Not Merely an Administrative Requirement, but a Strategic National Asset”: Dr. P. K. Mishra

AI and Advanced Analytics Can Strengthen Official Statistics, but Cannot Substitute for Quality of Statistics: Dr. P. K. Mishra

Dr. P. K. Mishra Delivers Keynote Address at Conference of State Planning, Finance and IT Secretaries Organised by MoSPI
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                13 OCT 2026 12:40PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister, Dr. P. K. Mishra, today delivered the keynote address at the inaugural session of the Conference of State Planning, Finance and IT Secretaries, organised by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) in New Delhi. Emphasising the importance of credible statistics, data harmonisation and technology-enabled governance, he said a strong statistical system is essential for evidence-based policymaking and achieving the vision of Viksit Bharat @ 2047.
Dr. Mishra said statistics, data, technology, planning and governance are increasingly interconnected elements of India’s development journey. A robust statistical system, he noted, must enable governments to measure development progress across States and districts, assess policy outcomes, identify gaps and ensure that public resources deliver the intended results. “What cannot be measured cannot be managed effectively. And what cannot be managed effectively cannot be transformed sustainably,” he observed.
Highlighting the need to modernise economic measurement, Dr. Mishra said India’s statistical systems must evolve alongside an economy that is increasingly digital, formalised and interconnected. He noted that the introduction of the new National Accounts Series, with 2022-23 as the base year, alongside updated Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Index of Industrial Production (IIP) series, represents an important step towards keeping statistical methodologies aligned with changing economic realities.
Underscoring the importance of State Statistical Systems, Dr. Mishra said India’s development story is fundamentally a story of its States, where policies are implemented, economic activity takes place and citizens experience development outcomes. He called for stronger institutional capacity and closer Centre–State coordination to improve the quality of official statistics.
Dr. Mishra said artificial intelligence, machine learning, geospatial systems, satellite imagery and advanced analytics offer significant opportunities to improve the timeliness, accuracy and usefulness of official statistics. However, he cautioned that technological advancement must remain guided by statistical quality, transparency, privacy, security and accountability. “Speed cannot come at the cost of accuracy. Greater use of data cannot come at the cost of confidentiality,” he said.
Dr. Mishra described statistics as an important instrument of cooperative federalism, enabling States and the Centre to compare outcomes, identify best practices and learn from regional differences. As India progresses towards 2047, he said, national averages alone would not suffice; granular data at State, district and local levels would be increasingly necessary to identify development gaps and guide interventions.
Concluding, Dr. Mishra called for a collective national effort involving MoSPI, State Statistical Offices, Finance, Planning and IT Departments, NITI Aayog, academic institutions and other stakeholders. He said India needs a statistical architecture that is trusted, transparent, technology-enabled, interoperable and policy-relevant. Such a system, he added, would not merely measure India’s transformation but also help guide and accelerate it towards Viksit Bharat @ 2047.

subtitle:

Building Grassroots Leadership: Dedicated iGOT Platform to Train and Certify Adi Karmayogi Volunteers Across India
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                13 OCT 2026 6:29PM by PIB Delhi
content:
A dedicated AKV microsite to build a trained and certified cadre of village-level volunteers for tribal development. The Ministry of Tribal Affairs (MoTA) and Karmayogi Bharat signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) today in New Delhi to develop and operate the Tribal Affairs Capacity Building Platform under the iGOT Karmayogi framework. The MoU extends the capacity-building framework of Mission Karmayogi, hitherto focused on civil servants, to Adi Karmayogi Volunteers (AKVs) and functionaries responsible for implementing tribal development schemes at the grassroots level.
The initiative is part of the Adi Karmayogi Abhiyan, under which the Ministry is institutionalising over 76,000 Adi Sewa Kendras (ASKs) and a network of over 1,54,000 AKVs as sustainable village-level platforms for facilitation, citizen engagement and last-mile convergence. According to data reported by States on the portal, 60,507 ASKs and 1,22,072 AKVs have been registered so far.
.
A Novel Intervention:
Through a dedicated AKV microsite on iGOT, every volunteer will have access to standardised, mobile-friendly learning resources that can be accessed anytime, anywhere. These resources will cover tribal development schemes and the volunteers’ roles and responsibilities in the field, with assessments and certification. The content can be updated centrally and disseminated to all volunteers simultaneously, while learning progress can be tracked State-wise.
Division of Roles:
Karmayogi Bharat will host, operate and maintain the platform, onboard learners, provide technical support and analytics, and report progress. MoTA, as the domain owner, will identify target groups and competencies, develop and approve content, nominate learners, and promote platform adoption. A joint Steering Committee will review progress and address implementation-related issues.
Linked to Field Training:
The platform will complement a three-day in-person training programme for AKVs, to be designed and delivered by State Administrative Training Institutes (ATIs) in partnership with State Tribal Welfare Departments. Four priority States—Maharashtra, Odisha, Goa and Tripura—are expected to complete the training by 31 October 2026, while all States are expected to complete it by 31 December 2026.
Progress So Far:
The AKV microsite is operational. Instructional videos have been disseminated through bulk SMS to over 1,25,000 AKVs, and the number of AKVs who have logged in and enrolled in courses has crossed 500. Orientation sessions for State ATIs have been completed, and sample training calendars and guidance materials have been shared with the institutes.
Speaking on the initiative, Smt. Ranjana Chopra, Secretary, Ministry of Tribal Affairs, Government of India, said:
“The Adi Karmayogi Microsite on iGOT Karmayogi is an important step towards democratising access to capacity building and strengthening grassroots leadership in tribal areas. With 646 course enrolments, 235 course completions and 112 Adi Karmayogi Volunteers having successfully completed at least one course, the platform is demonstrating encouraging initial engagement. By equipping community volunteers with knowledge of government schemes, service delivery mechanisms and citizen-centric governance, this initiative aims to transform Adi Sewa Kendras into effective last-mile institutions for tribal empowerment. As participation expands, the microsite will play a pivotal role in building a skilled, informed and responsive volunteer cadre, ensuring that the benefits of development reach even the remotest tribal habitations.”
The MoU reflects the vision of placing governance in the hands of local communities. Trained AKVs will help families access their entitlements, support the planning and monitoring of schemes, and strengthen convergence at the village level.
