content:
India's fight against tuberculosis has achieved significant milestones, with yearly emerging cases dipping by 21%, compared to the global decline of 12% between 2015 and 2024. India’s treatment coverage is 92% versus global coverage of 78%. Driven by the intensified TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, cumulative screenings have crossed 28.1 crore, with over 20 lakh individuals provided TB Preventive Treatment (TPT), 5.7 lakh new Nikshay Mitras added, and 46,118 Gram Panchayats awarded TB-free certification. The national response has been substantially accelerated through a 34-fold increase in X-ray screening via handheld units, the rollout of the TB Mukt Bharat App featuring the AI chatbot 'Khushi', and the introduction of the shorter, safer BPaLM (Bedaquiline, Pretomanid, Linezolid, and Moxifloxacin) treatment regimen for drug-resistant patients alongside advanced AI-driven triage tools. Building on this progress, the JOSH (Joint Squad for Health) campaign mobilises young people and communities to promote TB awareness, early detection, timely treatment, and treatment adherence, while addressing stigma. By strengthening community participation and collective action, the campaign reinforces the Jan Andolan approach towards achieving a TB-free India.
Introduction
India is on track towards tuberculosis elimination. New cases of tuberculosis emerging yearly in India have been reduced by 21% from 2015-2024 as compared to the global decline of 12%, according to the World Health Organisation’s Global Tuberculosis Report 2025. India’s treatment coverage is 92% versus global coverage of 78%.
This marks one of the most significant declines in TB incidence globally, exceeding the pace of reduction recorded in other high-burden nations. Deaths due to TB reduced by 28% during the same period. The Government of India’s targeted, multi-pronged approach towards detecting, screening and treating tuberculosis has contributed significantly to this progressive trend. Advanced technology expanded local health services, community engagement, and affordable treatment have put India on track to eliminate this prevalent and potentially fatal disease.
JOSH Campaign to Mobilise Communities Towards TB Elimination
To further amplify this momentum towards eliminating TB, a nationwide social media campaign featuring
JOSH (Joint Squad for Health) Teams
– across 11 states and 55 districts on a pilot basis – was organised on
13th October 2026
. Every JOSH team has MY BHARAT volunteers, cadets from the National Cadet Corps, and a designated Class-I officer to spread awareness on timely screening and treatment.
This structure mobilises the youth towards grassroots community awareness. All ministries, departments, healthcare institutions, MY Bharat volunteers and youth organisations, students and citizens are encouraged to join in amplifying TB awareness, early detection, treatment adherence and stigma-free communities through posts, photographs, videos and inspiring stories highlighting youth-led action.
The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare held workshops on the TB Mukt Abhiyaan with members of the Parliament and Legislative Assemblies. However, to take this campaign forward, involving the communities was deemed crucial. The JOSH campaign endeavours to be the next step in
increasing community participation
, highlighting the importance of screening and early detection. The campaign highlights the requirement for diagnosis and treatment, along with community participation, to increase active screening and to find asymptomatic patients.
This community participation and awareness building, particularly in vulnerable and marginalised populations, is crucial for removing fear and increasing awareness in people about treatment and screening as well. Together with the initiative, this campaign is aimed at making TB Mukt Bharat a reality through both institutional support and community mobilisation.
TB and Symptoms
What is Tuberculosis?
Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by a bacterium called
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
, usually impacting the lungs. TB can also affect other parts of the body, such as the brain, kidneys, or the spine.
A person infected by the bacterium may become sick, but some do not. Inactive TB cases or latent TB infections also exist. People with inactive TB may not spread the disease to others like those with an active TB infection– yet they may develop active TB anytime and become sick.
Babies and children, and people with weaker immune systems, are more likely to get sick
when infected. Without proper treatment,
active TB can be fatal
.
TB Symptoms
Symptoms of active TB are usually specific to the site affected by the bacteria, though there are some symptoms common to all types of TB.
People with active or symptomatic TB can spread the TB bacteria to others. When they cough, sneeze or speak, tiny droplets containing the bacteria can be released into the air and inhaled by people nearby—especially in spaces with poor ventilation.
Although tuberculosis spreads through the air, it does not transmit through:
Handshakes
Using public toilets
Sharing food and utensils
Everyday social interactions
Patients with lung TB generally stop being contagious after they have been on appropriate TB medicines for at least two weeks. People with TB in parts of the body other than the lungs usually cannot spread the disease.
What Should You Do If You Notice Symptoms?
The National TB Elimination Programme provides free screening and treatment services across the country at all public health facilities and many private healthcare centres, too. If you or anyone you know is showing TB symptoms:
Call the toll-free Ni-kshay Sampark TB& Hepatitis helpline: 1800-11-6666 for guidance and visit your nearest government health centre – TB diagnosis and treatment are provided free of cost under government programs.
You can also download the TB Aarogya Sathi app on your Android phone for more information on symptoms and nearby health facilities. The app helps you locate the closest centres offering TB diagnosis and treatment and provides guidance on medication side effects as well as nutritional advice for TB patients.
Strategic Plan to End TB in India
The Government is committed to eliminating tuberculosis (TB), in alignment with Sustainable Development Goal 3 (SDG 3), which seeks to ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all. The
National Strategic Plan to End TB in India 2020-25
, announced in June 2020, aims to eliminate tuberculosis through four pillars:
Build, Prevent, Detect, and Treat
. The plan focuses
on early diagnosis, reducing transmission, treating patients with appropriate drugs and regimens, and creating patient support systems
.
National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme
In
2020
, the Government of India renamed the Revised National Tuberculosis Control Program (RNTCP) to the
National TB Elimination Program (NTEP).
This reflects India’s goal to
eliminate tuberculosis before the global target of 2030.
The NTEP builds on the four pillars of the NSP:
Detect – Treat – Prevent – Build
. The key activities of the programme are:
Early diagnosis of individuals with TB through high-quality testing, and proactive community outreach to find missing cases in vulnerable populations.
Prompt treatment with quality-assured drugs and treatment regimens, including drug-resistant TB.
Engaging with patients seeking care in the private sector.
Patient-centric treatment support and nutrition interventions through direct benefit transfer and the Ni-kshay Mitra initiative.
Contact tracing and TB preventive treatment among household contacts, children, people living with HIV (PLHIV), and in high risk /vulnerable populations.
Airborne infection control measures.
Multi-sectoral response for addressing social determinants.
The government runs various programmes under NTEP.
Pradhan Mantri TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan
The Pradhan Mantri-TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan (TB-Free India Campaign) was launched on September 9, 2022, as an
additional key component of the NTEP
. This initiative was launched to unite people from all walks of life in a ‘Jan Andolan’ (people’s movement) and accelerate the nation’s progress towards eliminating TB. Its objectives are:
Provide Additional Support to TB Patients to improve treatment outcomes
Augment Community Involvement
Leverage Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)
Nikshay Poshan Yojana and the Ni-kshay Mitra Programme
TB patients must eat a high-protein diet to counteract the adverse side-effects of the treatment drugs. The Nikshay Poshan Yojana, launched in 2018, provides
financial assistance of Rs. 1,000 per month to each notified tuberculosis patient
. Since its launch in April 2018,
Rs.4,454.68 crores have been disbursed directly into the bank accounts of 1.38 crore beneficiaries.
TB treatment is long, lasting at least 6 months, and sometimes even longer. A Ni-kshay Mitra is a “TB Friend” or supporter who provides TB patients with help during this treatment period. A person, an NGO, corporations, religious and community groups, government officials and public figures can volunteer to be Ni-kshay Mitras.
The TB Friend provides
regular food baskets
to help patients reduce out-of-pocket expenditures. They can also provide
psychosocial support
by checking in regularly, and
vocational support
to help patients rebuild their lives after recovery.
As of November 12, 2025:
6,77,541 individuals and organisations,
as Ni-kshay Mitras, distributed
over 45 lakh food baskets to TB patients
.
Over 2 lakh MY Bharat volunteers
have come forward to serve as Ni-kshay Mitras. MY Bharat is an initiative by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports which connects 15-29-year-old people to various government departments, private organisations and civil-society partnerships to address real-world challenges and issues.
100-Day TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan
The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare launched one of India’s most intensive TB elimination drives called the 100-Day TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyan on 7th December 2024 in 347 high-priority districts across 33 States/UTs. To achieve early diagnosis of TB, vulnerability mapping and systematic screening of high-risk populations for TB were undertaken. The Jan Andolan also led to active involvement of over 30,000 elected representatives and 24 line ministries and support of Ni-kshay Mitras, exhibiting a whole-of-society and whole-of-government approach to TB elimination. The strategies of TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan have now been scaled up and expanded nationwide across all districts.
As of June 2026, the intensified campaign has crossed major milestones:
over 28.1 crore
people screened,
20 lakh individuals
provided TB Preventive Treatment (TPT), and
5.7 lakh new Nikshay Mitras added.
During the second phase of the campaign starting March 2026,
over 1.7 lakh Ayushman Arogya Shivirs
were held across
1.2 lakh high-risk villages
and wards,
backed by active participation from 32 lakh students and
1.9 lakh MY Bharat volunteers
.
The treatment success rate under the TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyan has
risen to 90%,
surpassing the global
average of 88%.
New Initiatives
New shorter, safer and highly effective
BPaLM regimen
having Bedaquiline, Pretomanid, Linezolid and Moxifloxacin has been introduced under the programme for drug-resistant TB patients, which will reduce the duration of treatment to 6 months. More than 15,000 MDR/RR-TB patients have been initiated on this regimen.
TB Preventive treatment:
Recognising that prevention is as critical as cure, TB Preventive Treatment (TPT) is provided to eligible beneficiaries to prevent the progression of TB infection to active disease. Through targeted and innovative approach, the programme has successfully protected household contacts and people living with HIV (PLHIV) over the years by administering TPT. The intervention has also been integrated with active and intensive case-finding campaigns and expansion to other vulnerable groups.
Ayushman Arogya Mandirs
Ayushman Arogya Mandirs are community health centres under the larger Ayushman Bharat scheme providing universal and affordable healthcare to all. There are 1,87,250 Ayushman Arogya Mandirs in India (as on October 13, 2026) – including sub-health centres, primary health centres, urban primary health centres, AYUSH (Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homeopathy) centres and Urban Health and Wellness Centres. People showing TB symptoms can go to these centres to get diagnosed.
Healthcare workers at an Ayushman Arogya Mandir in Himachal Pradesh's Kullu district screen women for TB and other diseases (September 20, 2025), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
Technological Infrastructure
More than 9800 rapid molecular testing facilities
and
107 culture and drug susceptibility testing
laboratories exist – the world’s largest network – for early TB detection and care. Other tools are:
Over 500 AI-enabled hand-held chest X-ray units
for community screening, with 1,500 being delivered to the states and union territories
Ni-kshay digital platform facilitates direct benefit transfer of nutritional support
34-Fold Surge in X-Ray Screening:
Driven by the large-scale deployment of handheld X-ray units nationwide.
TB Mukt Bharat App & 'Khushi' Chatbot:
A newly launched digital platform integrated with an AI-powered chatbot to track progress, guide citizens on symptoms, and locate nearby diagnostic centers.
Capacity Building:
The Ministry has expanded radiographer positions under the National Health Mission alongside expanding Truenat and CBNAAT diagnostic machinery.
Finding
TB
Cases
in
Remote
Kashmir
In the isolated Gurez valley of Bandipora District, Kashmir—located 2,400 metres high in the Himalayas
and
cut
off
during
winter-the
NTEP
Kashmir
team
conducted
an
intensive
TB screening campaign. Using mobile testing vans equipped with advanced diagnostic
machines and
portable
X-ray
equipment,
the
team
screened
1,250
people
over
three
days
and
identified over 250 potential TB cases for further testing. They also conducted awareness sessions with the Indian Army, local health workers, village representatives, and religious leaders. This effort reflects Jammu and Kashmir's commitment to achieving a “TB-free Kashmir” by 2025.
AI-Led Initiatives
The government is using AI systems for the detection, diagnosis, and treatment of tuberculosis in its push to integrate the technology into healthcare delivery to improve access and speed of care. These are:
Health
Focus
AI
Solution
/
Initiative
Process,              Technology
"Treatment"
Experience
&
Clinical
Impact
/      Operational
TB Screening
Cough Against       TB (CATB)
Acoustic AI: A 3-second recording of a patient's cough via smartphone app analyses frequency  patterns  for  TB
Signatures.
1.62+ Lakh screened; 12–16% extra yield in cases over conventional methods.
TB
Management
Adverse Outcome Prediction
Predictive Analytics: AI flags patients at high risk of treatment failure, once flagged treatment is
initiated.
Reported 27% decline in adverse outcomes after nationwide deployment.
TB Triage
DeepCXR (Chest X-ray)
Radiology AI: Automated reading of digital X-rays to identify  nodules/cavities  for
presumptive TB cases.
Deployed in 8 State/UTs; available free of cost to the  Govt  to  bypass
specialist shortages.
Gearing Towards Eliminating TB
India’s steady decline in TB incidence is a powerful reminder that sustained commitment, community participation, and strong public health initiatives truly make a difference. With continued vigilance, expanded access to care, and collective responsibility, the country is moving closer to a future where TB-free India is not just a goal, but an achievable reality. The JOSH social media campaign endeavours to increase TB awareness and help in mobilizing communities towards eliminating TB. Through these initiatives spanning healthcare institutions at all levels, the youth, and communities, India is gearing towards eliminating a dangerous and prevalent disease to create a Viksit Bharat 2047.

title: Khadi & Village Industries: From Tradition to Enterprise
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                13 OCT 2026 11:12AM by PIB Delhi
content:
A charkha spinning in a village once spoke of nationalism. Today, that spirit is taking new shape through a growing ecosystem of rural enterprises. Honey, herbal products, banana fibre, textiles and other village industries are creating new possibilities for traditional skills.
The spirit of self-reliance continues to resonate with the vision of
Vocal for Local and Atmanirbhar Bharat.
Traditional skills and local resources are finding new markets through access to finance, technology and training.
This growing connection between local enterprise and consumers is also reflected in the Khadi Mahotsav. The
Khadi Mahotsav takes place annually from 2 October to 31 October
. With a particular focus on youth, the campaign sensitises them towards Khadi and “Vocal for Local” and encourages the public to buy Khadi and local products.
At the centre of this transformation is the
Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC)
. It is a statutory body established under the Khadi and Village Industries Commission Act, 1956. The Act mandates KVIC to plan, promote, facilitate, organise and assist village industries. It covers measures related to
training, raw materials, marketing, research, and quality improvement
. It also supports skill development and research, while providing technical information and facilities related to Khadi and village industries.
In 2025–26, sales of Khadi and Village Industries products reached a historic ₹1.87lakh crore,
the highest level recorded (as of May 2026). Compared with 2013–14, sales grew by 501%, while production increased by 380% to ₹1,25,296 crore. Employment in the sector increased by 56% to 2.04 crore. The remuneration paid to artisans has also increased. It rose from ₹4 per hank in 2013–14 to ₹15 per hank currently, an increase of approximately 275%.
One hank is equivalent to 840 yards of yarn in length and one pound by weight.
Building Rural Businesses, One Artisan at a Time
From acquiring skills to accessing markets, a range of interventions is supporting artisans and village industries.
KVIC has a network of
35 departmental and non-departmental training centres
. Training covers food products, bakery, beekeeping, agarbatti, candles, motor repairing and several other activities. During FY 2025-26,
79,682 trainees
received training under various KVIC training programs.
Women
constitute more than
80% of approximately five lakh artisans
in the Khadi sector. In 2025–26,
47,382 women
received training under various KVIC programmes, accounting for approximately 59% of all trainees.
Training is complemented by interventions including toolkit and equipment distribution, marketing support and other measures.
Since March 2008, the
Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP)
has provided employment opportunities to nearly 97.95 lakh people through KVIC.
One such beneficiary is Shri Jitendra Baitha, who established a bakery products manufacturing unit in Bihar in 2020. His venture has an annual turnover of ₹72 lakh and currently provides employment to 20 people, in the local community.
Support also includes enterprise finance and the tools and technology needed for production.
The
Gramodyog Vikas Yojana
empowers artisans by providing modern machines, toolkits and equipment. During 2025–26, 37,769 such machines, toolkits and equipment were distributed. KVIC, under the scheme, has distributed more than 3.23 lakh machines, toolkits and equipment (May 2026).
These efforts are complemented by measures that strengthen the wider ecosystem in which Khadi institutions and artisans operate.
The
Khadi Vikas Yojana
helps Khadi institutions improve products, add value and respond to changing market demand. Its
Modified Market Development Assistance
provides greater flexibility for value addition and market-oriented pricing. During 2024–25, ₹245 crore was disbursed to 1,097 Khadi Institutions, benefiting 1,45,484 artisans.
Access to affordable credit adds another layer of support. Under the
Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate Scheme
, eligible Khadi institutions can access credit at a concessional interest rate of 4% per annum.
For artisans, the workplace itself also matters. The
Workshed Scheme
provides improved production spaces and a more congenial working environment. During 2025–26, up to December 2025, 1,309 artisans benefited under the scheme.
These measures support artisans with improved working conditions and access to resources for production.
From Village Enterprises to Wider Markets
Across village industries, traditional skills and local resources are being developed into new businesses and products, supported by technology, training and market linkages. Research and development efforts are strengthening productivity, quality and competitiveness.
Shri S.P. Singh built his enterprise around
honey and cookies,
with support under the
PMEGP scheme through KVIC
. Based in Punjab, his business now provides employment to around 200 workers and exports its products to international markets. Honey and cookies are among its key products, with the United States accounting for a major share of exports.
After receiving support in 2010, the enterprise gradually expanded its export presence through participation in international exhibitions.
KVIC facilitated participation in exhibitions across Dubai, the United States and the Middle East, helping the enterprise connect with overseas buyers.
Today, the business exports to 36 countries and is developing a second unit in Rajpura, Punjab, to expand honey exports to European markets.
For
Shri B. Sundaraj
, a naturally fragrant plant became the foundation for a village enterprise. Through his Agarbathi Unit, he produces agarbatti, herbal products, Vetiver Agarbathi and Vetiver Samburani. With support under the Gramodyog Vikas Yojana (GVY) during 2024-25, he strengthened his manufacturing capabilities and diversified his product range. This enables him to develop multiple value-added products from a locally available resource. His enterprise illustrates how
KVIC support can help translate traditional knowledge and local resources into marketable village industry products.
In Jatti Majra village of
Solan district, Himachal Pradesh
, Shri Sahil Chaudhary runs a mono-carton manufacturing unit. The enterprise caters to construction and packaging requirements in the region.
Established with a project cost of ₹25 lakh, the unit operates under KVIC-supported PMEGP.
The enterprise now records an annual turnover of around ₹45 lakh and provides employment to 23 people. The financial assistance helped translate Chaudhary’s entrepreneurial idea into a functioning manufacturing enterprise. His journey illustrates how local entrepreneurship can contribute to self-reliance, employment and the broader vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat.
Opening New Markets for Village Enterprises
KVIC has expanded both digital and physical channels for reaching consumers. It has an online Khadi India store (
www.khadiindia.gov.in
) offering a range of products, including clothing and fabrics, grocery, beauty products, essential oils, perfumes and incense sticks.
The Khadi India brand is supported through dedicated publicity and marketing initiatives. These efforts connect traditional products with contemporary consumers. The marketing network extends across the country. It includes
8 departmental Khadi India sales outlets and 15 KVIC branches.
Khadi Institutions operate another 8,035 sales outlets nationwide.
National, zonal, state and district exhibitions
provide additional market opportunities. KVIC also promotes participation in domestic and international trade fairs.
Khadi: Weaving a Global Story
Khadi is finding new expressions in fashion, with its distinctive craftsmanship showcased at platforms such as
New Zealand Fashion Week 2026 and Lakmé Fashion Week 2025
. In these events, the heritage techniques were brought together with contemporary designs to create a distinctly modern identity.
From Heritage to Opportunity
The growth of Khadi and Village Industries is reflected in
higher production and sales, expanding employment, increased artisan remuneration and new rural businesses
. As traditional skills connect with technology, finance and markets, the sector continues to open new avenues for enterprise across rural India.
